title: Those With No Tribe at Their Backs • That Noon of Scorching Sand • Ahad, Ahad • The Day Abu Bakr (RA) Settled the Price • The Remaining Names • A Father’s Objection, and the Answer from the Heavens • Zinnirah’s Eyes

blocks.0: Those With No Tribe at Their Backs
blocks.1: In the last dars we saw what came down upon the Prophet {{1}} himself. Abuse. Mockery. Thorns on the road. Entrails on his back in prostration. But there is one thing. No one was able to kill him. Why could they not!
blocks.2: There is really only one reason; Allah was protecting him. Allah Himself had told him that He would protect him from people.{{1}}
blocks.3: In the outward view, one form this protection took was the tribe. Banu Hashim stood behind him. Abu Talib was there. The rule of Arabia was simple; if anyone lays a hand on a man, his tribe will demand an accounting for his blood. For one man a whole tribe would raise swords. So Makkah was able to humiliate him, but did not dare to kill him openly.
blocks.4: But the tribe is only a means. The one whom Allah protects, no one can harm, whether or not a tribe stands behind him. Now ask the question the other way round. What would have happened to someone with no tribe behind him!
blocks.7: Those who accepted Islam in Makkah can be divided into three groups. One group, whose tribe was strong. Abu Bakr, ‘Uthman, al-Zubayr (RA). To lay a hand on them meant trouble. Their share was social boycott, humiliation, loss in business.
blocks.8: Another group, whose tribe existed but was weak. Hands were laid on them, but with measure. And the third group. Slaves. Slave-women. Freed slaves. Outsiders who had come from abroad. Those with no one behind them.
blocks.9: What came down upon these had no measure. In Arab society a slave was not a human being; he was property. Like a camel, like a sword, like the furniture of a house. The master could sell him, beat him, even kill him. No one would ask. For if someone kills his own camel, who will ask!
blocks.10: The call of Islam reached these very people. And the most astonishing thing is this; they were the first to answer. Those who had nothing to lose agreed to give everything. And those who had everything could not accept one thing. Because for these no one would come to ask for an accounting of blood.
blocks.11: Has the rule changed! In the office, the boy whose father is influential, no one raises their voice at him. And the boy who has come from the village, who has no place to stay, for whom losing the job means going hungry; anything can be said to him.
blocks.12: In the madrasa, the student whose guardian regularly checks on him is not touched. And the orphan, whom no one comes to visit; anything can be said about him.
blocks.13: At home, the girl whose father’s house is strong is spoken to in a lowered voice. And the one who has no father, no brother, no place to return to; she can be kept silent.
blocks.14: Jahiliyyah has not gone anywhere. The name of the tribe has changed into money, position, identity, the phone list. But the rule is the same. In what tone we speak to whom is decided by who stands behind him. One voice for the rickshaw-puller, another voice for the big boss at the office. Both are human. Why does the tone change! Only the name of the tribe has changed.
blocks.15: The person you can scold most easily today, why are you scolding him! Because he has done wrong, or because no one stands behind him! Let the question stay in your mind.
blocks.16: One more thing. Those whom Allah hears most readily are exactly these people. For the one who has no one behind him, He Himself is behind him.
blocks.18: The noon of Makkah. A noon when one cannot stand barefoot on the ground. The sand so hot that meat is scorched. Exactly that hour was chosen. Umayyah ibn Khalaf would drag out his slave. His name was Bilal. Bilal ibn Rabah. Of Abyssinian descent, a slave bought by Umayyah.
blocks.19: He would be thrown on his back on that burning sand. Then a huge rock would be lifted onto his chest. A rock of such a kind that moving beneath it was out of the question.
blocks.20: Umayyah would say, this is how you will die. If you want to live, disown Muhammad, and worship al-Lat and al-‘Uzza.{{1}}
blocks.21: The scene is like this. Beneath the back, sand like fire. On the chest, the weight of a rock. No room to draw breath. And standing over him, one man; whether the rock stays or is removed is in his hand. All he wants is a single word.
blocks.22: Just say one word and the rock is lifted. Shade is found. Water is found. When we read such events, we read them very easily. Two lines, then the next event.
blocks.23: The man lies on the sand. His back is burning. The rock on his chest is such that the lungs cannot fill with air. The sun is right in his eyes. And the man standing in front says, one word. Just say one word.
blocks.24: If I were on that sand, what would I have said! I know the honest answer myself. And that very answer is the true measure of my faith.
blocks.26: Bilal (RA) did not say that word. What came out of his mouth was one thing only. Ahad. Ahad. One. He is One. The more rocks pressed down, the more that one word. The more blows fell, the more that one word.
blocks.27: He gave no speech. He offered no argument. He did not weep. One word. Again and again. For when a person has nothing else left, what remains is his true wealth. Bilal had nothing in his hands. No house, no tribe, no money, not even his own body was his own. He had only one thing.
blocks.28: That, no one could snatch away. There is something else. He did not say ‘La ilaha illa Allah’ in full. He had no strength to. With a rock on the chest one cannot say a whole sentence.
blocks.29: So whatever he could, that much he said. One word. Ahad. Allah did not ask for the whole sentence. He asked as much as was within his capacity. We often think, if I cannot do it all, there is no point doing it. I cannot memorise the whole Qur’an, so I do not even begin. I cannot keep all my prayers, so I do not take hold of even one.
blocks.30: Bilal (RA) tells us otherwise. Hold fast to whatever you can. Allah knows the rest.
blocks.31: The Day Abu Bakr (RA) Settled the Price
blocks.32: One day Abu Bakr (RA) was passing that way. Seeing the scene, he stopped. He said to Umayyah, do you not fear Allah! How long will you treat this helpless man like this!
blocks.33: Umayyah said, you are the one who ruined him. Now you rescue him. Abu Bakr (RA) said, then sell him to me. Whatever price you want.
blocks.34: Umayyah named a steep price. Abu Bakr (RA) paid it without prolonging the talk. Umayyah thought he had won. A half-dead, broken slave sent off at a high price. Profit in business.
blocks.35: And Abu Bakr (RA) was thinking, I got him cheap. The same deal. Both think they have won. Who won, the whole world knows today. Where the ledger is opened, that is the real matter.
blocks.36: He bought Bilal (RA), and then immediately set him free.{{1}}
blocks.38: Bilal is not alone. Abu Bakr (RA) bought and freed seven persecuted slaves, men and women, in Makkah; four of them women.{{1}}
blocks.39: In a society where women counted for nothing, the names of four slave-women have been written for fourteen hundred years. And the names of those who beat them, no one remembered.
blocks.40: Where is our ledger opened! At month’s end we count the figure of the salary. The land deed, the bank papers, the son’s results; we count it all. And for what will be of use in the Hereafter, there is no ledger at all.
blocks.41: Umayyah counted too. The shiny price that came into his hand, a good deal. Only the ledger was opened in the wrong place.
blocks.43: Let us say a little about some of the seven whom Abu Bakr (RA) freed. Nahdiyah (RA) and her daughter; both were slave-women of a woman of Banu ‘Abd al-Dar. That mistress made them grind flour for her, and would say, by Allah, I will never free you.
blocks.44: One day the word of that oath reached Abu Bakr (RA). He said, break the oath. The mistress said, you are the one who ruined them, you free them. A deal was made. They were freed.
blocks.45: Umm ‘Ubays (RA). A slave-woman of Banu Zuhrah. She too was bought and freed. And ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA). He was a shepherd; he grazed goats. After being freed he grazed the goats of Abu Bakr (RA). Later, on the night of the Hijrah, he would bring milk on the way to the cave of Thawr, and with the flock of goats wipe out the footprints.{{1}}
blocks.46: Just reckon it. The man whom Makkah had kept at the work of grazing goats, on the most important night in history, that same man was wiping out the footprints of the Prophet {{1}}. Whom Allah will put to which task is beyond people’s reckoning.
blocks.47: Hearing these names, a thought comes. All of them were people on the lowest rung of society. A shepherd. A flour-grinding slave-woman. A blacksmith. Today there are exactly such people in our homes or around us.
blocks.48: The one who mops the house. The one who drives a rickshaw. The shop employee. The doorman. We do not know their names. When the need is over, we forget. Yet in Allah’s ledger perhaps his name comes first.
blocks.49: The Prophet {{1}} said, many a person with dishevelled hair, covered in dust, is turned away from doors; yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.{{2}}
blocks.50: This week do one thing. The person whose help you take every day yet whose name you do not know, learn his name. Then call him once by name.
blocks.51: A Father’s Objection, and the Answer from the Heavens
blocks.52: Abu Bakr’s (RA) father, Abu Quhafah, had not yet accepted Islam. Seeing his son’s spending, he was annoyed. He said, son, you are buying only weak slaves. If you are going to spend so much money, buy strong men; they will stand by you, they will protect you.
blocks.53: Abu Bakr’s (RA) answer was a single sentence. He said, I want what I want.{{1}}
blocks.54: The father is reckoning profit. The son is reckoning elsewhere. The father says, buy someone who will be of use to you. The son says, I am buying someone who has nothing to give me.
blocks.55: Right here is the definition of ikhlas. A gift where there is a chance of return is a transaction. A gift where there is no way at all of return, that is giving. The answer came down from the heavens
blocks.57: And the most pious will be kept far away from it, who gives his wealth (in the way of Allah) to attain purification, though no one had done him a favour that required repayment, rather he seeks only the pleasure of his Lord, the Most High. Be assured, such a person will soon be well pleased.{{1}}
blocks.59: The word in the verse is important here. ‘Though no one had done him a favour that required repayment.’ That is, from those whom he bought he had no dues whatsoever. Nor ever would. That very thing became the reason for praise in the verse.
blocks.60: The measure of ikhlas is right here. Allah does not first look at how big the deed is. He first looks at whether a way was open before me to get something from this world in exchange. The more that way is closed, the purer the deed.
blocks.61: Abu Quhafah was saying, buy someone who will be of use in the future. Abu Bakr (RA) chose exactly the opposite kind of people; no tribe, no power, no prospect of ever being of use. The door of getting anything back he kept shut on purpose.
blocks.62: There is one more thing. Abu Quhafah was a polytheist then. He did not understand his son’s deed, nor was he expected to. Yet Abu Bakr (RA) did not get entangled in argument with his father. He ended the talk in a single sentence.
blocks.63: When the people of the house do not understand the work of the din, there are two paths. One, trying to explain by arguing; which often ends in quarrelling. Two, carrying on with the work, and not spoiling the relationship.
blocks.64: He chose the second. And in the end that same father accepted Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah. Now let us look at ourselves. Where do we spend money! We go to the invitation that builds connections. To the son’s wedding of the man who holds power, we send a gift. At the function where our name will be announced, we give a donation.
blocks.65: And the person who will never be able to give anything! We do give him, but the leftover portion. Not the main portion. Abu Bakr (RA) did exactly the opposite. He gave the main portion to people who had nothing to give back.
blocks.66: Ask yourself one question. To whom did I give my last gift! And can that person ever be of any use to me! If the answer is ‘yes’, then perhaps it was not charity.
blocks.67: There is one more point. Abu Bakr (RA) did not merely give money. He made a decision. The decision was, I will stand beside a person by whose side standing brings me no gain.
blocks.68: Many people have money. Not everyone has the decision. Today, with whatever is in my hands, that decision can be made. A phone call. A recommendation. Some time. Going and sitting beside someone once.
blocks.69: The price is not the point. For whom I give, that is the point.
blocks.71: Zinnirah (RA) was a slave-woman. She was beaten so much that her eyesight went. The Quraysh laughed and said, see, al-Lat and al-‘Uzza have taken her eyes.
blocks.72: The blind woman answered. She said, that is false. Al-Lat and al-‘Uzza can neither benefit anyone nor harm anyone. This has come from the heavens; and if my Lord wills, He can return my eyes too.
blocks.73: The next morning her sight returned.{{1}}
blocks.74: The Quraysh said, Muhammad’s magic. Again the same words. When the moon split they say magic. When a blind eye is restored they say magic. For the eye that does not want to see, bringing light before it is no use.
blocks.75: But there is something else. A slave-woman who went blind from being beaten, standing and proving the creed of all Makkah wrong. In her hand there is no power. The argument is there.
blocks.76: And one more point, small but deep. The woman who lost her eyes did not say, give me my eyes back. She said, if my Lord wills, He can return them. Between the two sentences a whole faith stands. One a demand, the other a surrender. She did not demand the eye; she left the asking in Allah’s hands.
blocks.77: The next morning her eyes had come back. Had they not, her words would not have changed one bit. This is exactly where we get stuck in du‘a. We work out an account in our heads; I did this much, now I should get this. Then if we do not get it, we sulk, and give up du‘a.
blocks.78: Zinnirah (RA) was not one to sulk. She did not become truthful because her eyes returned; the truth was bigger to her than her eyes.

footnotes.0: Surah al-Ma’idah, verse 67, final part; ‘wa-Llahu ya‘simuka mina al-nas’, that is, ‘Allah will protect you from people’. Although the verse was revealed in the Madinan period, it is a declaration of the overall protection of the Prophet {{1}}; even in the Makkan period there were several attempts to kill him, and each time they failed. Translation: Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an.
footnotes.1: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–318; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 3/232–234. That Bilal (RA) was the slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf and accepted Islam in the earliest period is universally accepted in the Sirah and Tabaqat works. As for the part ‘he would be laid on his back on hot sand with a heavy rock placed on his chest, yet only one word would be on his lips; Ahad, Ahad’, it is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham through Ibn Ishaq; it has no chain from a Companion, so this part is mursal. Acceptable as a scene, not as proof in matters of creed.
footnotes.2: That Abu Bakr (RA) bought with money and freed many persecuted slave men and women, this general point is alluded to in the Qur’an at the end of Surah al-Layl; the details are in Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Tabari, in the tafsir of Surah al-Layl. The incident of buying Bilal (RA) and freeing him at once is narrated through Ibn Ishaq in Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–319; this part is mursal. There is variation in the reports about the price; in one source mention of a monetary price, in another the exchange of a disbelieving slave. In keeping with the allusion of Surah al-Layl, ‘gives his wealth’, the report of buying with money has been adopted here.
footnotes.3: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/317–320. ‘Abu Bakr (RA) bought and freed seven: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Zinnirah, Nahdiyah and her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays, and the slave-woman of Banu Mu’ammil (Lubaynah) (RA)’; this list of names and the number ‘seven’ are the narration of Ibn Hisham; this part is mursal. In other sources there is slight variation in the list of names.
footnotes.4: The persecution of Nahdiyah, her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays and ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA), and the account of their release at the hands of Abu Bakr (RA), appear in Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/319–320 and in Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; this part is mursal. Regarding the role of ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA) at the cave of Thawr, two parts need to be separated. The part ‘when part of the night had passed he would come near the cave with the flock of goats, and they drank milk’ is narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3905, from ‘A’ishah (RA); this has been verified on hadithunlocked.com. And the part ‘he would drive the flock and wipe out the footprints’ is not explicit in that hadith; it is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham through Ibn Ishaq, and this part is mursal.
footnotes.5: Sahih Muslim, hadith 2622; from Abu Hurayrah (RA). ‘Rubba ash‘atha aghbara madfu‘in bil-abwab, law aqsama ‘ala Llahi la-abarrahu’; that is, many a person with dishevelled hair, covered in dust, is turned away from doors, yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.
footnotes.6: That Abu Quhafah had still not accepted Islam and later accepted Islam on the day of the conquest of Makkah is established by sound chains. And the dialogue, ‘he said to his son, why are you buying the weak slaves; buy strong men, they will protect you; in reply Abu Bakr (RA) said, I want what I want’, is the narration of Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/320, through Ibn Ishaq, and of Tafsir Ibn Kathir (tafsir of Surah al-Layl); this part is mursal.
footnotes.8: In Tafsir Tawdih al-Qur’an, in the note on Surah al-Layl it is stated: according to some reports these verses were revealed in praise of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA); but the words of the verses are general, so this glad tiding applies to all who acquire this quality. See Tafsir Ibn Kathir and Tafsir al-Tabari, Surah al-Layl.
footnotes.9: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/319–320. That Zinnirah (RA) was one of the persecuted and that Abu Bakr (RA) freed her is well known in the Sirah works. And the part ‘she lost her sight from the beatings; the Quraysh said, al-Lat and al-‘Uzza have taken her eyes; she replied, they can neither benefit nor harm; the next day Allah restored her sight’ is the narration of Ibn Hisham; it has no chain from a Companion, so this part is mursal. Acceptable as a scene, not as proof for creed or karamat.

quiz.q: Why could no one kill the Prophet ﷺ in Makkah?
o: Allah was protecting him
The Quraysh held back for fear of Banu Hashim
He always stayed hidden
Bloodshed was forbidden within the precincts of the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: The real protection was Allah’s; He Himself had said that He would protect him from people (Surah al-Ma’idah 67). The tribe was only an outward form of that protection.

quiz.q: According to the dars, what did the degree of persecution depend on?
o: How deep a person’s faith was
Whether he gave da‘wah openly or not
Whether the protection of a tribe stood behind him
How old he was and how strong in body
quiz.e: Where the tribe was strong, boycott and humiliation; where the tribe was weak, beating with measure; where there was no tribe, there was no measure at all. This was the pattern of the persecution.

quiz.q: What question does the dars give for examining in what tone we speak to whom?
o: Has he done wrong, or does he have no one behind him
Exactly how grave is his wrong
Is he higher than me in rank
Will he in the end listen to what I say
quiz.e: One voice for the rickshaw-puller, another voice for the big boss; both are human. The reason the tone changes is itself the real question.

quiz.q: Who was the master of Bilal (RA)?
o: Abu Jahl
al-‘As ibn Wa’il al-Sahmi
Umayyah ibn Khalaf
Umm Anmar
quiz.e: Umayyah ibn Khalaf would throw him on his back on the scorching sand at noon and place a heavy rock on his chest.

quiz.q: With the rock on his chest, which word came to the lips of Bilal (RA)?
o: La ilaha illa Allah
Ahad, Ahad
Allahu akbar
Hasbuna Allah
quiz.e: He had no strength to say the whole sentence; so whatever he could, that much he said. ‘Ahad’ means one; He is One.

quiz.q: What is the dars’s answer to the thought, ‘I cannot do it all, so I will not even begin’?
o: Swap it for an easier deed
Begin only after making full preparation
Hold fast to whatever you can
Begin with the help of others
quiz.e: With a rock on the chest one cannot say the whole kalimah; so one word. Allah did not ask for the whole, He asked for what was within capacity. The rest He knows.

quiz.q: How did Abu Bakr (RA) rescue Bilal (RA)?
o: Secretly took him away
Complained in the assembly of the Quraysh
Went to the Prophet ﷺ and asked for intercession
Bought him for a price and set him free
quiz.e: Abu Bakr (RA) said, sell him to me, whatever price you want. Umayyah named a steep price and he paid it; then he set Bilal (RA) free.

quiz.q: How many persecuted slave men and women did Abu Bakr (RA) buy and free in Makkah?
o: Three
Seven
Five
Nine
quiz.e: Bilal, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Zinnirah, Nahdiyah and her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays, and the slave-woman of Banu Mu’ammil; seven in all. Four of them were women.

quiz.q: What is the significance of four of the seven being women?
o: Women were the most persecuted
Their names remained even in a society that kept no account of women
Buying and freeing male slaves was harder
The price of slave-women was comparatively much lower
quiz.e: The names of those who beat them, no one remembered; and the names of four slave-women have been written for fourteen hundred years.

quiz.q: What work did ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah (RA) do after being freed?
o: Traded in the caravans of the Quraysh
Gave the adhan in the mosque of Makkah
Grazed the goats of Abu Bakr (RA)
Earned his living by ironwork
quiz.e: He was a shepherd. On the night of the Hijrah he brought goat’s milk to the cave of Thawr; this account is in Sahih al-Bukhari.

quiz.q: What does the dars ask us to do about the person whose help we take every day yet whose name we do not know?
o: Give him extra payment
Learn his name and call him by name
Make du‘a for him
Reduce his workload
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, many a dusty person is turned away from doors, yet if he were to swear by Allah, Allah would fulfil it.

quiz.q: What advice did Abu Quhafah give his son?
o: To buy strong slaves, who would be of use
To stop buying slaves and save the money
To put the money to work in trade and increase it
To come to a settlement with the Quraysh
quiz.e: The father was reckoning profit; the son was reckoning elsewhere. The answer was a single sentence: I want what I want.

quiz.q: In praise of Abu Bakr (RA), verses of which surah are reported to have been revealed?
o: Surah al-‘Ankabut
Surah al-Buruj
Surah al-Layl
Surah al-Nahl
quiz.e: Verses 17–21 of Surah al-Layl. According to the note of Tawdih al-Qur’an the words of the verses are general, so this glad tiding is for all who acquire the quality.

quiz.q: Why did the Qur’an praise the giving of Abu Bakr (RA) in particular?
o: Because he gave a great deal of wealth
Because he gave openly in front of everyone
Because he gave on the direct command of the Prophet ﷺ
Because those to whom he gave had nothing to give back
quiz.e: The words of the verse: ‘though no one had done him a favour that required repayment.’ A gift where there is no way of return is giving; the rest is a transaction.

quiz.q: What was Abu Bakr’s (RA) way when the people of the house did not understand the work of the din?
o: It is good to get into a long argument with reasoning
Carry on with the work, without spoiling the relationship
Hold the work back for a few days
Leave the house and go somewhere else
quiz.e: He ended the talk in one sentence and did not get into argument. And that same father accepted Islam in the end, on the day of the conquest of Makkah.

quiz.q: What is the measure for checking whether one’s gift is truly giving?
o: Whether the one I gave to will ever be of use to me
Whether it was given openly or in secret
Whether the amount was big enough
Whether it is given every month regularly
quiz.e: A gift where there is a chance of return is a transaction. A gift where there is no way of return is giving; the verse of Surah al-Layl says exactly that.

quiz.q: How can the principle of Abu Bakr (RA) be followed even with modest means in hand?
o: Save up and give one big sum at once
Donate to the fund of some institution
Encourage others to give
Stand by someone with a phone call or a recommendation
quiz.e: Many people have money; not everyone has the decision. The price is not the point; for whom I give, that is the point.

quiz.q: What happened in the case of Zinnirah (RA)?
o: She was driven out of Makkah
She was tortured with hot iron
All her wealth was seized
She lost her sight from beatings, and it later returned
quiz.e: The Quraysh said that al-Lat and al-‘Uzza had taken her eyes. She replied, they can neither benefit nor harm. The next day her sight returned.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the condition ‘if He wills’ in the answer of Zinnirah (RA)?
o: It draws the line between faith and demand
It is merely a rule of du‘a
It is a way of avoiding a prophecy
It is just a language of humility
quiz.e: She did not demand her eyes back. She did not become truthful because her eyes returned; she would have been even had they not. In du‘a, this is the very condition we forget.
